summary: Provides state machine tables for LDP processing on ATM switch label switching routers. The LDP specification had no state machine, and a common one helps different LDP and CR-LDP implementations work together. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The LDP specification says what each message means, but not exactly what a router should do when it arrives. This memo supplies the missing part for ATM routers: the states a label switched path moves through, the events that trigger each move, and what the router does in each state. Its purpose is that two implementations behave the same way.

questions: what is the ldp state machine
what states does an ldp lsp have
what is vc merge in mpls
what is downstream on demand label distribution
subtitle: State tables that say exactly how an ATM switch reacts to each LDP message while building label switched paths.

tldr.problem: The LDP specification says what each message means but not what a router does in between, so two implementations can disagree about what to do when a request arrives or a mapping comes back.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives state machine tables for ATM label switching routers: the states an LSP control block moves through, the events that cause each move, and the action taken in each state. It covers downstream-on-demand mode with and without VC-merge, and downstream unsolicited mode.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and an extension to the LDP specification, which it does not override. The authors say a common state machine matters for interoperability between LDP and CR-LDP implementations.

today: RFC 3215 is an Informational memo that extends the LDP specification, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It says the state machines clarify procedures in RFC 3036 and do not override them, and that security considerations about spurious internal events are not addressed.

sections.title: Why a Common State Machine
sections.content:
The memo provides state machine tables for ATM switch label switching routers. In the current LDP specification there is no state machine specified for processing LDP messages, and the authors think that defining a common state machine is very important for interoperability between different LDP and CR-LDP implementations.

The focus is on the LDP state machines and the associated control blocks used for establishing and maintaining label switched paths. State machines for the LDP controller, which is in charge of LDP session initialization, address mapping message management and the routing interface, are not described, because they are defined in the LDP specification. Even though the state machines here are specific to an ATM label switching router, the authors say they can be easily adapted for other types of router.

The message names used throughout are short. LDP-REQUEST is the Label Request message, LDP-MAPPING the Label Mapping message, LDP-WITHDRAW the Label Withdraw message, LDP-RELEASE the Label Release message, LDP-ABORT the Abort message used to abort a path setup, and LDP-NAK the Notification message used to reject an LDP message.
sections.plainLanguage: The LDP specification had the messages but not the rules for reacting to them. Two routers could read the same specification and still behave differently, which is exactly what breaks an interoperability. This memo writes the reactions down as tables.

sections.title: Control Blocks, States and Events
sections.content:
Two sets of state machines are provided: one for an ATM router that does not have VC-merge capability and one for an ATM router that does. The descriptions are given in terms of control blocks, states, events, response actions and state transitions. Control blocks contain the information required to handle events, and may hold additional information needed by a specific implementation or by the procedures in the LDP specification and the objects in the LDP MIB. The state machines cover both independent path control and ordered path control.

For each path there are two kinds of state machine in the non-VC-merge case. The LSP Control Block and its state machine handle normal path setup; it is created when the router receives a new request and deleted when that path is torn down. The Next Hop Trigger Control Block and its state machine handle switching over to a better path through a different next hop; it is created when the router decides to switch and deleted when the switch is finished. That machine uses a timer, and has corresponding states, so that the switch happens in a timely fashion after a routing transient has had time to stabilize.

The LSP Control Block may hold the upstream and downstream label request identifiers, that is the Message Id in the request received from upstream and the Message Id in the request sent downstream, the upstream and downstream LDP identifiers, the state, the FEC, the upstream label assigned by this router, the downstream label assigned by the downstream router, a pointer to the trigger control block that sets up or tears down the path, used only at the ingress router, and a pointer to the control block used for switching to a better next hop. Four index combinations locate a unique LSP Control Block: the downstream label and downstream LDP identifier, the upstream label and upstream LDP identifier, the downstream label request ID and downstream LDP identifier, or the upstream label request ID and upstream LDP identifier.

The states are IDLE, the initial state when the control block is created; RESPONSE_AWAITED, meaning the router has received and processed a request from upstream or an internal setup request, has sent a new request downstream, and is waiting for the mapping; ESTABLISHED, meaning the mapping has arrived from downstream and the path is up and operational; and RELEASE_AWAITED, meaning the router has sent a withdraw upstream and is waiting for the release before freeing the label resource.

The events are the messages arriving and the local decisions: LDP Request from upstream, LDP Mapping from downstream, LDP Release from upstream, LDP Withdraw from downstream, LDP Abort from upstream, LDP NAK from downstream, losing the LDP session with an upstream or a downstream peer, an internal set up, for example a configuration request for a traffic engineering tunnel or recognizing a new FEC, an internal destroy, an internal cross-connect used to splice two paths into one when switching to a better next hop, and an internal new next hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Each path has a record that holds the labels, the identifiers and the current state. The record moves between four states, and what moves it are the six message types plus a handful of local decisions such as tearing a path down or switching to a better route.

sections.title: The LSP State Transitions
sections.content:
The transition diagram starts at IDLE. An LDP Request or an internal set up moves the router to RESPONSE_AWAITED, and an LDP Release, an LDP Abort from upstream, an internal destroy, or losing the upstream session moves it back to IDLE.

In RESPONSE_AWAITED, an LDP Mapping moves the router to ESTABLISHED. A downstream NAK or losing the downstream session moves it back to IDLE. The diagram also shows a second LDP Request leaving RESPONSE_AWAITED, which is the ordered control case, where the router sends a request to the next downstream router and waits for its own downstream to answer.

In ESTABLISHED, an LDP Withdraw or an internal destroy moves the router to RELEASE_AWAITED, where a further withdraw or losing the downstream session also leads. From RELEASE_AWAITED, an LDP Release, an upstream abort or losing the upstream session returns the router to IDLE.

The actions in each state follow from the same picture. In IDLE, on an LDP Request, if the router is the egress or proxy egress for the path it chooses an upstream label, connects it to the local IP forwarding module, allocates the resources, sends the mapping upstream and goes to ESTABLISHED. Otherwise it obtains a next hop or interface for the FEC named in the request, propagates the request with a newly assigned message ID towards that next hop, and goes to RESPONSE_AWAITED. If the router uses the independent control mode it instead chooses an upstream label, connects it to the forwarding module, goes to ESTABLISHED and sends the mapping upstream. If the request cannot be processed for any reason, it issues an NAK to the sender with the appropriate error code, stays in IDLE and deletes the control block.
sections.plainLanguage: The path is idle until someone asks for a label. The router then asks the next router downstream and waits. When the mapping arrives the path is up, and when it comes down again the router withdraws the label upstream and waits for the release before reusing it.

sections.title: Handling a Next Hop Change
sections.content:
When there is a topology change and a router detects a better next hop for a path, it may behave in two ways. It can try a local repair, extending the path through the new next hop, releasing the old path from this router forward and then splicing into the newly extended path. Or, if the path was created with the pinned option used by CR-LDP, the router ignores the new next hop change and the path stays unchanged, though it may send a mapping containing attributes for the new next hop that have changed.

The next hop trigger control block holds the state, a pointer to the original LSP control block, and a pointer to the LSP control block that is setting up a path through the new next hop. Its states are IDLE, the initial state when the block is created; NEW_NH_RETRY, where the router waits for a retry timer to expire and then tries to establish a path through the new next hop; and NEW_NH_RESPONSE_AWAITED, where the router is in the middle of establishing that path, having triggered a control block to send a request towards the new next hop and waiting for the mapping.

The events are all internal: a new next hop detected, a retry timeout, the path to the new next hop being up, the path through the new next hop not getting set up, and a destroy, which is triggered when the router loses the LDP session with its upstream neighbour. A new next hop moves the machine from IDLE to NEW_NH_RETRY, the retry timeout moves it to NEW_NH_RESPONSE_AWAITED, and the path coming up or failing moves it back to IDLE. A destroy at any point also returns it to IDLE.
sections.plainLanguage: When the route improves, the router sets up a second path alongside the first and waits to see whether it works. A timer keeps the attempt from starting too early, while the routing settles, and the original path is only torn down once the new one is up.

sections.title: Other Variants: VC-Merge and Downstream Unsolicited
sections.content:
Section 2.3 covers an ATM router that can merge virtual circuits. A VC-merge capable router can map several incoming labels into one outgoing label, but it may only be able to merge a limited number: a node capable of merging four incoming labels into one, with six incoming labels arriving for a FEC, may merge them into two outgoing labels. When an upstream router has a limited merging capability it is difficult for a downstream router to know how many labels should be assigned to each FEC, and in that case downstream-on-demand is recommended.

Three kinds of control block are involved there: an Upstream LSP Control Block for each request received, a Downstream LSP Control Block for each unique request sent to a downstream router, and a Next Hop Trigger Control Block for each FEC where a better next hop has been detected. A downstream block holds pointers to the upstream blocks it is serving, which is how the router says that several incoming labels map to one outgoing label.

Section 3 gives the state machines for the router in downstream unsolicited mode, where labels are pushed to the upstream router rather than requested. Only the ordered path control mode is taken into account there, because the independent mode uses liberal label retention and is considered to burn too many ATM resources. Multiple paths are not supported in this version and are left for further study, with the authors suspecting that multiple next hops in downstream mode make it easy to get into a loop condition.

Two kinds of control block are involved. There is a list of upstream blocks for each FEC in the routing table, one for each LDP peer, created when there is a label ready to distribute upstream and deleted when the FEC is deleted, the peer disappears, or the downstream label is withdrawn. There is one downstream block for each FEC in the routing table, created when the FEC is inserted into the forwarding table and deleted when it is removed from it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two variants change the shape of the machine. A router that merges several upstream labels into one downstream label needs extra records to keep track of which upstream labels belong to which downstream label. A router that pushes labels without being asked has a simpler job, because it does not have to wait for anyone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo is an informational extension of the LDP specification. The state machines are intended to clarify procedures defined there, but do not supplant or override them. Implementations of a state machine may be vulnerable to spurious events generated by an external source, and the events here fall into two categories: internal events and external events caused by receipt of an LDP message.

LDP messages may be protected using the mechanisms described in the LDP specification. Security considerations relating to the generation of spurious internal events are not addressed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds no security of its own. It points at the LDP specification for protecting the messages, and says nothing about a router being fed events that no one meant to send.

items.title: LSP Control Block

items.title: Next Hop Trigger Control Block
items.text: Holds the pointers used for switching a path to a better next hop.

items.title: LDP-REQUEST
items.text: The Label Request message, asking a downstream router for a label.

items.title: LDP-MAPPING
items.text: The Label Mapping message, carrying the label downstream.

items.title: LDP-WITHDRAW
items.text: The Label Withdraw message, taking a label back.

items.title: LDP-RELEASE
items.text: The Label Release message, giving a label up.

items.title: LDP-ABORT
items.text: The Abort message, used to abort a path setup.

items.title: LDP-NAK
items.text: The Notification message, used to reject an LDP message.
